Six things that belong in your audit binder before fieldwork starts, in the order an auditor will ask for them:

1. Trial balance with prior-year comparison, signed by the CFO or Finance lead.
2. Schedule of net assets with donor restrictions, with a roll-forward of additions, releases, and ending balance per fund.
3. Grant agreements for every active award, including modifications and amendments. Originals, not summaries.
4. Schedule of expenditures of federal awards (SEFA) if you crossed the $1,000,000 single audit threshold. With ALN numbers, pass-through identifiers, and direct vs pass-through breakouts.
5. Board minutes for the audit period, with motions related to budget approval, restricted fund designations, and any related-party disclosures highlighted.
6. Bank reconciliations for every month, with the reconciler and reviewer initialed.

The binder is not the audit. It is the artifact that proves the audit can move quickly.

If item two takes more than a day to assemble, you do not have a reporting problem. You have a system-of-record problem.

[image suggestion: a flat-lay photograph of a tabbed audit binder with the six section labels visible, on a desk with a coffee cup. Warm light, no stock-photo people.]

Quick check: when did you last reconcile your SF-425 cash drawn against your general ledger?

If the answer is "at the next FFR deadline," that is the audit finding waiting to happen.

Reconcile monthly. The variance is always smaller than you expect when you catch it early.

Reconciling a donor CRM to the general ledger can surface three patterns: payments booked to the wrong fund, pledges entered twice, restricted gifts coded as unrestricted.

None of these are unusual. All three surface only when someone compares the two systems row by row.

The quiet cost of running parallel systems is not the integration tax. It is the recurring two-week reconciliation that shows up before every audit, every board meeting, and every 990. The work that produces no new value, only confidence that the existing values are correct.

If you are doing that reconciliation more than once a year, the system count is too high.

Three places a grant can live simultaneously:

1. The donor CRM, where the funder is a contact and the award is a soft-credit row.
2. QuickBooks, where the dollars hit a class or a fund code.
3. A spreadsheet, where the actual reporting deadlines and budget categories sit.

None of these is wrong. They are each doing one job well.

The problem is that no one of them tells you where the grant stands. To answer "how much of the Clinic Capacity award is left, and what is due next," someone has to stitch all three together.

That stitching is the work. It happens at month-end, at board prep, at audit time, at every report deadline. It is the tax you pay for not having the three things in one place.

Five things a federal program officer can ask for with no warning, that should not require a fire drill.

1. Current cumulative draw against the award, by budget category. Federal share only.

2. The last three months of payroll allocation across this award, with time and effort certifications attached.

3. A list of any cost transfers between budget categories during the period, with the supporting memo for each.

4. Sub-recipient invoices and the monitoring activity you performed before paying them.

5. The most recent SF-425 (FFR) you submitted, plus the reconciliation between it and the GL.

If any of these takes more than 30 minutes to assemble, the underlying record-keeping has drifted from what 2 CFR 200 expects. The call is a signal, not the problem.

If you are an Executive Director heading into a Monday board meeting with a finance subcommittee question on restricted fund balances, the print-out you want is the Schedule of Activity by Net Asset Class.

Opening balance, additions, releases from restriction, ending balance. Per fund. One page.

Not the full GL. Not the YTD P&L. The schedule.

If a federal program officer called this morning and asked for your Q2 SF-425 numbers, how long until you could read them out?

Be honest. Are they in the accounting system, a working spreadsheet, or three places that do not match?

The FFR (Federal Financial Report, formerly SF-425) wants cash receipts, cash disbursements, federal share of expenditures, and obligations as of the report date. Cash basis, accrual basis, or both, depending on the award.

An org can rebuild it given a week. The actual job is being able to answer in 10 minutes, the day the call comes, with numbers your auditor will not flag in the fall.

That gap (between "we can produce it" and "we can produce it on demand") is where compliance risk hides.

A question for executive directors at $500K-$10M nonprofits: how long does board prep currently take, and how many systems does the staff touch to assemble the packet?

The pattern is consistent. Revenue year-to-date comes from QuickBooks. Pipeline status comes from a CRM or a spreadsheet. Retention metrics come from a different report. Restricted fund balances come from QuickBooks classes if they exist or a spreadsheet if they do not. Compliance deadlines live in Outlook or one staff member's head.

When each number reconciles differently, assembling a packet that holds up under board scrutiny takes a full week. The ED often does it personally because no one else has context across every system.

Mid-sized nonprofits spend an average of 20 to 30 percent of staff time on compliance data entry across at least 12 different reporting systems per the Center for an Urban Future January 2023 research.

Organizations that compress board prep from a week to an afternoon do it the same way: one system holding donor, grant, restricted fund, and compliance data, with reports generated from live data rather than assembled the night before.

A youth program managing 21st Century Community Learning Centers funds, an AmeriCorps grant, and two foundation grants is operating four separate compliance frameworks simultaneously.

21st CCLC compliance is not only financial — it requires participant attendance tracking, outcome reporting (teacher surveys, grade progression data), and demographic records submitted to both the federal Department of Education and the state education agency. The state layer varies significantly: some states require quarterly submissions, others semi-annual. The format and data requirements differ by state.

AmeriCorps compliance runs through Corporation for National and Community Service systems — a separate portal, separate member hour tracking, and prohibited activities compliance that has nothing to do with 21st CCLC documentation.

Foundation grants add a third reporting format and a third deadline calendar.

For a lean program team — often one director managing 15 part-time program staff — this is not a coordination problem that more effort solves. It is a systems problem. The complexity of tracking multiple federal compliance frameworks simultaneously exceeds what any individual can manage manually without documentation failures.

36% of nonprofits ended FY2024 with an operating deficit, the highest rate in a decade. Administrative overhead in multi-grant environments is part of that pressure.

Youth programs carrying federal grants need compliance infrastructure, not just a spreadsheet with color-coded deadlines.

Matching funds: the term nonprofits misunderstand most often.


Under 2 CFR 200.306, match contributions must be non-federal, verifiable from your records, necessary and reasonable for the project, allowable under applicable cost principles, and included in the approved budget. All five requirements apply simultaneously.


The most common audit finding: using another federal grant as match. A HUD CDBG grant cannot match a HOME grant. An AmeriCorps award cannot match an HHS program. The prohibition is strict, with narrow statutory exceptions that most nonprofits do not qualify for.


The second most common problem: in-kind match that was not documented contemporaneously. Volunteer hours estimated at year-end based on memory do not satisfy the requirement. Volunteer hours logged weekly, with position descriptions and market rate comparisons, do.


A 1:1 match on a $500,000 federal award means the grantee must contribute $500,000 in non-federal resources — cash, in-kind, or a combination. Falling short is a compliance violation reportable in a Single Audit and can result in a proportional reduction of the federal award.


One more trap: voluntary committed match. If you pledged match beyond the minimum in your application to improve competitiveness, that commitment is legally binding once it appears in the award agreement. An auditor will test it.


#matchingfunds #grantcompliance #federalgrants #uniformguidance

Under 2 CFR 200.430, payroll charges to federal awards must be supported by after-the-fact records reflecting actual time worked — not budget percentages. Personnel costs are 65-75% of expenditures on most human services awards and the largest single category of disallowed costs in federal Single Audits.


The two-system problem is where this falls apart. Payroll runs in ADP or QuickBooks. The grants manager keeps a salary allocation spreadsheet. Finance posts journal entries to move costs from a general payroll account to grant-specific accounts. The time-and-effort certifications are PDFs in a shared folder. At audit time, the auditor wants three things lined up — the certification, the allocation entry matching the certification, and the payroll register confirming gross pay. Reconciling three sources for every employee, every month, every award, is the manual work that consumes days and still leaves gaps.


The most common finding is allocation percentages that do not match the certified time — usually because the allocation was entered at budget percentages instead of certified ones. The second most common is late certifications signed more than 30 days after period end. Both create dollar-for-dollar repayment exposure.


GrantPipe records salary and fringe allocations directly to grant ledgers per pay period, links each entry to the corresponding time-and-effort certification, flags percentage mismatches before audit, and supports CSV imports from ADP, Paychex, and QuickBooks Payroll.


#payrollallocation #2cfr200430 #grantcompliance #federalgrants

Development directors at $2M–$10M nonprofits typically carry 40 to 120 major donor prospects in active moves management alongside 8 to 25 active grants at any given time.


The Fundraising Effectiveness Project has reported sector-wide donor retention between 40 and 45 percent every year for over a decade. The cause is rarely appeal quality. It is the failure to follow up the second gift, track the lapsed-donor list, or notice when a multi-year pledge is 90 days overdue. These are operational failures — ones that fragmented tooling makes routine.


Most development directors run four systems that do not talk to each other: a donor CRM for gift history, a spreadsheet for the grant pipeline, QuickBooks for restricted fund balances, and a slide deck for the board that requires manually joining all three. Reconciling across those systems to build a board packet consumes 4 to 8 hours per cycle. If the CFO's numbers and the development report disagree, the development director explains it at a board meeting.


The job that needs doing is not complicated: moves management, grant pipeline, restricted fund visibility, and board-ready reporting from one source of truth.

After-school nonprofits managing 21st Century Community Learning Centers grants face a quarterly reporting requirement that no standard donor CRM or general-purpose accounting system was built to handle.

The 21st CCLC program distributed approximately $1.3 billion in federal grants in fiscal year 2023, serving more than 1.7 million students at 6,600 centers operated primarily by nonprofits.

Quarterly attendance reporting requires documentation by school, grade level, and program type — data that lives in a student enrollment database, not a financial system. Annual academic outcome reporting requires teacher survey data, grade progression rates, and test score linkage coordinated with partner schools.

Title I pass-through funds add a second compliance layer. The funding chain runs from the U.S. Department of Education to the state to the local school district to the nonprofit. Each tier adds conditions: allowable use restrictions, district review and approval requirements, reimbursement billing rather than advance payments, and state monitoring visits.

Then there are split grant cycles. School-year programs often run on an academic calendar while summer programs run under a calendar-year or state fiscal-year grant. When those cycles do not align with the organization's fiscal year, every funder report requires manually reconstructing expenditures for a period that crosses fiscal year boundaries.

These are structural compliance challenges, not administrative problems a spreadsheet solves.

EPA awarded approximately $3.6 billion in environmental justice grants under the Inflation Reduction Act. Individual nonprofit grants ranged from $100,000 to $20 million.

Each of those awards comes with compliance requirements that go beyond standard nonprofit financial reporting.

EPA grants require environmental outcome metrics alongside financial data — community engagement counts, environmental improvements measured, program reach figures. There is no standard template for these in most nonprofit accounting systems. Tracking outcomes separately from financial records creates reconciliation work at every reporting period.

A significant portion of EPA funding reaches nonprofits through state environmental agencies as pass-through sub-awards. That structure means dual compliance: file reports with the state in the state's format, while maintaining documentation that meets federal audit standards if the award is reviewed at the federal level. Procurement rules, conflict-of-interest policies, and Title VI civil rights compliance requirements flow through from EPA to the sub-recipient.

USDA NRCS conservation grants — particularly through the Regional Conservation Partnership Program, which obligated over $4 billion in FY2023 — add project-phase complexity. Annual financial reports must document expenditures by phase, tied to approved budget line items and conservation plan milestones.

Most environmental nonprofits manage this compliance load with general-purpose tools that were not designed for it.

Quick check: when was the last time someone on your team confirmed the period of performance dates on every active federal award?

Not the award amount. The dates. Start date, end date, allowable pre-award costs, allowable extensions.

That is usually where audit findings live.

Before: a Development Director enters a $50,000 multi-year pledge in the donor CRM as a single record. The Finance Director booked $25,000 this fiscal year and $25,000 next. The 990 prep team asks which version is right. Both answers are partially right.

After: the pledge lives once. It carries the donor, the restriction language, the schedule, and the conditional clauses. Finance and Development read the same record. The 990 prep team pulls a report instead of asking a question.

The shape of the data has to match the shape of the work. A pledge is not a transaction. It is a schedule of obligations a donor has made and a schedule of receivables an organization has accepted. Treating it as a row in a CRM is how you end up with three different correct answers.

Quick check: do you know which restricted funds are scheduled to release this quarter?

Not the total balance. The release schedule. The dates donors and grant makers tied their dollars to.

If the answer requires a meeting with Finance, the workflow is the question.

$1,000,000.

That is the federal expenditure threshold that triggers a Single Audit under 2 CFR 200 Subpart F.

If your federal expenditures in a fiscal year cross that line, you owe a Single Audit. A separate engagement, with its own report on internal controls, its own report on compliance, and its own Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (SEFA).

The line is on expenditures, not awards. A $1.2M three-year award that spends $400K per year stays under each year. A $400K award plus a $400K pass-through plus $50K in smaller awards crosses it.

Orgs can cross by accident, in a year where a pass-through draws down faster than expected. Model the threshold before the fiscal year ends.

[image suggestion: simple chart showing federal expenditures stacked across multiple awards, with a horizontal line at $1M labeled "Single Audit threshold"]

Under 2 CFR 200.430, employees on multiple federal awards cannot use semi-annual time certification — but most organizations apply it to them anyway.

Semi-annual certification is permitted only for employees working solely on a single federal award or cost objective. An employee working 80% on one federal award and 20% on administrative duties does not qualify. Monthly certification is required for that employee.

Auditors know this rule and test for it by looking at how employees are classified and whether the certification frequency matches the classification. It is one of the most reliable single-audit findings in the personnel cost category.

The correct process: pull a list of every employee with federal grant charges for the period, determine certification frequency based on whether they are single-award or multi-award, distribute certification forms within two weeks of month-end, collect and review for completeness, then reconcile certification percentages to posted payroll allocations.

That reconciliation step — comparing what employees certified against what payroll actually posted — is the control that makes the entire system credible. Filing certifications without reconciling provides no assurance.

Certifications requested 90 days after the period they cover are reconstructions from memory. Auditors can tell the difference.

Before issuing a sub-award, the first question to answer in writing is: is this organization a subrecipient or a contractor?

The 2 CFR 200.331 five-factor test determines the classification. Subrecipient indicators include: the entity determines who is eligible for the federal assistance, its performance is measured against federal program objectives, it has programmatic decision-making responsibility, it is accountable for federal compliance requirements, and it uses the funds to carry out its own program.

Contractor indicators are the opposite: the entity provides goods or services in normal business operations, serves many purchasers, operates in a competitive market, and is not subject to federal program compliance requirements.

The classification matters because the monitoring obligations in 2 CFR 200.332 — pre-award risk assessment, ongoing financial report review, documentation desk review for medium/high-risk organizations, site visits for high-risk subrecipients, and fac.gov single audit verification for organizations expending $1,000,000 or more in federal awards — apply to subrecipients, not contractors.

A free subrecipient monitoring checklist covering every step under 2 CFR 200.332 — pre-award risk assessment through file documentation requirements — is available at https://lnkd.in/eznJK6Za.

A mid-sized veterans service organization may simultaneously manage VA SSVF grants, DOL Homeless Veterans Reintegration Program funding, and HUD-VASH service contracts — each with different compliance frameworks, performance metrics, and audit standards.

VA SSVF grants require veteran status verification before funds are expended on behalf of any participant. That means a DD-214 or equivalent documentation, income eligibility documentation, and housing status documentation in the case file before the first dollar is charged.

DOL veterans employment grants require something different: tracking job placements, wages at placement, and employment retention at the 2nd quarter and 4th quarter after placement. That is an ongoing data collection obligation that extends months beyond the service period.

When a case manager's time is split across VA-funded and DOL-funded activities, that cost must be allocated to the correct program — documented and defensible under two different compliance frameworks simultaneously.

The VA awarded approximately $490 million in SSVF grants to community organizations in FY2023. The documentation requirements that come with those awards are not incidental to the compliance process. They are the compliance process.

Organizations that cannot produce complete veteran eligibility files during a site visit face findings. The documentation must exist before the auditor asks.

To the Executive Director who has been quoted five-figure implementation fees for a Salesforce NPSP implementation, plus annual license costs on top, plus a part-time admin to keep it running:

The license price is the smallest number on the invoice.

Real cost lines on a typical NPSP rollout for a $3M nonprofit:

- Implementation partner: tens of thousands in implementation fees
- Licenses: per-user license fees on top, plus add-ons
- Admin time: 10 to 15 hours a week, indefinitely
- Re-implementation in year 3 when the original consultant moves on

What you bought was a platform. What you needed was a product. Those are not the same thing.

If your team spends more time configuring the system than using it, the system is the project. The grants and the donors are the side quest.

Myth: "Our CRM handles grants, so we're covered."

Neon CRM's base platform covers donor management and fundraising. Restricted fund tracking, expenditure reporting tied to individual grants, and compliance documentation are not standard features — they require custom configuration or a separate tool.

This is not unique to Neon CRM. Most donor CRMs were not built for the post-award compliance layer. They track contacts, gifts, and pipelines. They do not track grant budget balances by award, generate SF-425 data, or flag when a budget line is about to be overrun.

The gap shows up during audit season and at grant closeout. Staff need documentation of how restricted funds were spent. A donor CRM without grant compliance functionality cannot produce that documentation without a manual reconstruction.

A mid-sized nonprofit managing both donor relationships and restricted grants needs to know what those two workflows require — and whether the same platform handles both or only one.

Requesting an itemized quote that covers your actual feature list — not just the base subscription — is the only accurate way to budget.

NTEN's 2024 Security Survey found 46% of nonprofits reported a data breach or unauthorized access incident in the past three years. Improper access controls were the leading contributing factor.


Salesforce NPSP implementations average $15,000-$50,000 in consulting fees just for permission and security model configuration. The platforms are flexible, but configuring them correctly requires expertise most nonprofit operations staff do not have.


The result: organizations leave default permissions in place because locking it down requires a consultant.


GrantPipe uses three roles — Admin, Editor, Viewer — that cover every legitimate access pattern for nonprofit operations. Role assignment is two fields and takes effect immediately. No support ticket, no setup project.


Board members get Viewer access for dashboards. Program staff get Editor access to update grant milestones. The audit trail logs every create, edit, and delete by user and timestamp.


Staff turnover at nonprofits runs 20-30% annually. Simpler permission systems handle the recurring deprovisioning work more reliably.


#nonprofitcrm #permissions #datasecurity #grantpipe

Questioned costs.


Defined at 2 CFR 200.516, a questioned cost is an expenditure flagged during a single audit because it appears unallowable, unsupported, or unreasonable.


Three categories. Unallowable: violates statute, regulation, or terms of the award. Unsupported: missing documentation. Unreasonable: exceeds what a prudent person would incur in similar circumstances.


The reporting threshold is $25,000 per federal program. When questioned costs attributable to a single program exceed that, they are listed in the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs.


Two examples that show up frequently. An auditor finds $32,000 in payroll charged to a federal award without time-and-effort documentation — reported as unsupported, exceeds threshold. A nonprofit charges $18,000 in alcohol-related catering to a training grant — unallowable, under threshold, still disclosed.


Questioned costs are not automatic disallowances. The pass-through entity or federal agency makes the final determination. The audit just flags them.


#singleaudit #grantcompliance #2cfr200 #federalgrants

Donorbox at $300,000/year in donations costs $5,250 in platform fees alone. At $400,000/year it costs $7,000.


The free tier is genuinely free — no monthly subscription. The 1.75% platform fee is deducted from each donation. Donorbox Pro at $199/month waives the fee on the first $1,000/month of donations.


What Donorbox does well: embeddable donation forms deploy in hours, recurring gift management with a donor-facing portal for payment updates, and zero setup friction for organizations without a software budget.


What it does not do at any tier: full donor CRM with moves management, major gift officer assignment, restricted fund tracking, or grant lifecycle management. Donorbox Pro adds basic CRM features, but they remain shallow relative to purpose-built CRMs.


Donorbox has processed over $2 billion across 50,000+ nonprofits. The product is good at what it does. The problem is total cost of ownership shifts as donation volume grows past roughly $200,000 annually, where the fee model starts crossing the cost of a dedicated CRM with grant compliance built in.


The break-even calculation is rarely run until the organization is already past it.

If your Development Director left tomorrow, who would know which grant reports are due in June?

Not in theory. In practice. Whose laptop has the funder portal logins. Whose inbox has the program officer's last email. Whose head holds the unwritten rule that this funder wants narrative before financials.

At a $500K to $10M nonprofit, the grant function often comes down to one person. Sometimes two. The deadline calendar lives where the work happens, which is wherever that one person works.

This is not a software problem first. It is a documentation problem. But software can make the documentation a side effect of the work instead of a separate task that never gets done.

Sunday is a good day to write down the next 90 days of grant deadlines, the funder, the report type, and the portal URL. One page. Shared drive. Done.

If the person who knows this is reading: the page is for the version of you that gets the flu in week two of June.

We decided early that grants and funds had to be separate database entities. Not the same thing with a flag.

A grant is an award. It has a funder, a period of performance, a budget, reporting deadlines, and a closeout date. It is a contract.

A fund is a bucket of restricted dollars. It can be funded by one grant, by multiple grants, by a private gift, or by a board designation. The restriction sits on the fund.

A single program (say, Youth STEM) can pull from a federal pass-through grant, a foundation grant, and a private donor's restricted gift. Three sources, one fund, one set of allowable costs to track.

If you model that as one table with a "type" column, you spend the rest of the product's life writing exceptions. We modeled it as two tables connected by an allocation table. Boring. Correct. Matches FASB ASC 958 and how Sage Intacct does it.

Most CRMs do not separate these because they did not start in fund accounting. That is fine for tracking gifts. It is not fine for closing a federal award.

Picture this: three different versions of the same grant budget at a Development office. One in QuickBooks, one in a Google Sheet, one in the donor CRM. None of them are wrong. They are all incomplete.

The QuickBooks version has the GL detail but no funder reporting categories.

The Sheet has the funder categories but the actuals are a month stale.

The CRM has the award amount and the contact but no spend data at all.

Three systems, one truth split into thirds. The hand-off between Development and Finance happens by copying numbers between tabs. Every quarter. By a person whose actual job is something else.

Single source of truth is not a slogan. It is the moment one number stops needing reconciliation.

Most "audit prep" advice tells you to start in August. That is too late.

The audit binder is not a document you assemble. It is a byproduct of how you ran the year. If your evidence trail only exists when an auditor asks for it, you do not have an evidence trail. You have a scramble.

Here is the inversion. The week-by-week version of audit prep is not 14 frantic weeks before fieldwork. It is 52 quiet weeks that produce a binder as a side effect.

What that looks like in practice:

Each award has a folder with the executed agreement, the approved budget, every amendment, and the board minutes that authorized it. That folder gets touched on day one and never restructured.

Each drawdown gets a memo. One paragraph. Date, amount, period covered, the GL accounts it ties to. Filed in the award folder when the cash hits.

Each personnel allocation gets a certification at the cadence the funder requires. Federal awards under 2 CFR 200.430 require after-the-fact certification that payroll charges reflect actual work. Frequency varies by agency and funding structure. Filed in the award folder, not in HR.

Each sub-recipient sends back a quarterly compliance attestation. Filed in the award folder. Read by someone, not just received.

When fieldwork starts, the binder is already built. The auditor's PBC list is a retrieval task, not a manufacturing task.

This is the difference between organizations that dread audit week and organizations that schedule it like a dental cleaning. The work was done in the months before. May and June are the right months to set it up for the next cycle.

ALN: Assistance Listing Number. The federal program identifier you used to call CFDA.

The number itself did not change when the name did in 2018. 14.218 is still CDBG Entitlement Grants. 93.243 is still SAMHSA's Projects for Assistance in Transition from Homelessness.

If your award letter says CFDA, the funder is using old paperwork. The number is still valid. Match it on assistancelistings.gov to confirm program details before you cite it in a board memo.

Quick check before Monday: do you know your organization's UEI expiration date?

SAM.gov registrations renew every 12 months. If yours lapses in the middle of a draw request, the federal payment system will reject the drawdown. Not delay it. Reject it.

The renewal window opens 60 days before expiration. Missing this surfaces at the worst time: when SAM.gov support is unavailable.

Two minutes on sam.gov this week. Search your entity, note the expiration date, set a calendar reminder for 60 days prior.

That is the whole task. It just has to happen.

Questioned costs.


Defined at 2 CFR 200.516, a questioned cost is an expenditure flagged during a single audit because it appears unallowable, unsupported, or unreasonable.


Three categories. Unallowable: violates statute, regulation, or terms of the award. Unsupported: missing documentation. Unreasonable: exceeds what a prudent person would incur in similar circumstances.


The reporting threshold is $25,000 per federal program. When questioned costs attributable to a single program exceed that, they are listed in the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs.


Two examples that show up frequently. An auditor finds $32,000 in payroll charged to a federal award without time-and-effort documentation — reported as unsupported, exceeds threshold. A nonprofit charges $18,000 in alcohol-related catering to a training grant — unallowable, under threshold, still disclosed.


Questioned costs are not automatic disallowances. The pass-through entity or federal agency makes the final determination. The audit just flags them.

Three reasons restricted-fund tracking breaks in donor CRMs:

One. Restrictions are properties of the gift, not the donor. A single donor can give a restricted gift this year and an unrestricted gift next. CRMs index on the donor first.

Two. Releases from restriction are events, not statuses. When the Youth STEM program spends $4,200 of a $50,000 restricted grant, that is a release event with a date, an amount, and a reference to the underlying expense. Most CRMs have no event model for this.

Three. The schedule of activity is a financial statement disclosure. It needs to roll up by net asset class, by restriction type, and by fund. CRMs report by donor, by campaign, by appeal. Different axes.

This is not a CRM critique. It is a fit observation. The CRM does what it was built to do. Restricted fund accounting is not on that list.

Matching funds: the term nonprofits misunderstand most often.


Under 2 CFR 200.306, match contributions must be non-federal, verifiable from your records, necessary and reasonable for the project, allowable under applicable cost principles, and included in the approved budget. All five requirements apply simultaneously.


The most common audit finding: using another federal grant as match. A HUD CDBG grant cannot match a HOME grant. An AmeriCorps award cannot match an HHS program. The prohibition is strict, with narrow statutory exceptions that most nonprofits do not qualify for.


The second most common problem: in-kind match that was not documented contemporaneously. Volunteer hours estimated at year-end based on memory do not satisfy the requirement. Volunteer hours logged weekly, with position descriptions and market rate comparisons, do.


A 1:1 match on a $500,000 federal award means the grantee must contribute $500,000 in non-federal resources — cash, in-kind, or a combination. Falling short is a compliance violation reportable in a Single Audit and can result in a proportional reduction of the federal award.


One more trap: voluntary committed match. If you pledged match beyond the minimum in your application to improve competitiveness, that commitment is legally binding once it appears in the award agreement. An auditor will test it.


#matchingfunds #grantcompliance #federalgrants #uniformguidance

We decided early that grants and funds had to be separate database entities. Not the same thing with a flag.

A grant is an award. It has a funder, a period of performance, a budget, reporting deadlines, and a closeout date. It is a contract.

A fund is a bucket of restricted dollars. It can be funded by one grant, by multiple grants, by a private gift, or by a board designation. The restriction sits on the fund.

A single program (say, Youth STEM) can pull from a federal pass-through grant, a foundation grant, and a private donor's restricted gift. Three sources, one fund, one set of allowable costs to track.

If you model that as one table with a "type" column, you spend the rest of the product's life writing exceptions. We modeled it as two tables connected by an allocation table. Boring. Correct. Matches FASB ASC 958 and how Sage Intacct does it.

Most CRMs do not separate these because they did not start in fund accounting. That is fine for tracking gifts. It is not fine for closing a federal award.

USDA Rural Development administers over $20 billion in loans, loan guarantees, and grants annually across three mission areas — and each program has its own authorizing statute, compliance requirements, and eligible activity definitions.

A nonprofit managing Community Facilities grants, Rural Business Development Grants, and REAP energy grants simultaneously is not managing one compliance framework. It is managing three, on top of standard 2 CFR 200 Uniform Guidance.

The geographic eligibility problem compounds this: all USDA Rural Development programs require that funded activities benefit rural areas, defined by population thresholds that vary by program. Communities near urban boundaries can lose eligibility between decennial census updates. Rural area eligibility is not a one-time determination — it is an ongoing documentation obligation.

EDA Public Works grants add a multi-year tracking requirement on top: job creation and private investment outcomes must be documented at specific intervals, typically five years after project completion. A grant that closed five years ago still has reporting obligations.

Rural development nonprofits often face this compliance burden with two or three administrative staff covering multi-county service areas. The documentation requirements were written for program densities that do not reflect rural operational reality.

What compliance infrastructure does your rural development organization have in place for geographic eligibility documentation across multi-county programs?

A $3M nonprofit typically runs Bloomerang for donors, QuickBooks Online for accounting, a spreadsheet for grants, Google Workspace for documents, and a separate payroll system.


That stack is normal. It is also where the operations manager's week disappears.


The role's effectiveness correlates almost perfectly with the fragmentation of the toolset the staff uses. Every extra system is another integration, another vendor renewal, another set of permissions, another place audit evidence might live.


The question for ops managers reading this: if you wrote down every system the development, finance, and program teams touch in a normal week, how many show up?


For most $500K to $10M nonprofits the count lands between 8 and 14.


What is the one consolidation that would actually free up the most time — not the most license cost, the most time?

A Single Audit finding is not a disaster. A weak Corrective Action Plan response is.


Under 2 CFR 200.511(c), every finding requires a written CAP with five required elements: the finding reference number, the auditee's position (agree or disagree), the specific corrective action, the name and title of the responsible party, and the target completion date.


"Management will strengthen its procurement controls" does not meet that standard. It will invite awarding-agency follow-up and likely result in additional reporting requirements.


A strong CAP reads like a project plan: "The CFO will update the procurement policy by May 31, circulate it to all staff with a signed attestation, and provide completed attestations to the audit committee at the June meeting."


Completion dates should be aggressive but achievable — typically 30 to 180 days. Missed CAP deadlines are themselves a finding risk in the following audit.


Repeat findings in two or more consecutive audits trigger specific conditions under 2 CFR 200.208: prior approval for draws, enhanced monitoring, or high-risk designation. Breaking that pattern often requires more structural change than the first response suggested.


Disagreeing with a finding is legitimate. Unsupported disagreement damages credibility with both the auditor and the awarding agency.
